clue.text: Australia tried enthusiastically removing England's openers – harsh!

indicators.note: openers are the things that start, so only the first letter of each preceding word is wanted

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for Australia
the initial letter of each of these four words

explanation.surface: An Australian side plays its heart out and gets rid of England's opening batsmen, which feels harsh to English fans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'England's openers' reads like cricket batsmen, but 'openers' governs all four words before it, taking each one's first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Austere and harsh are synonyms for something severe, stern or lacking in comfort.

clue.text: Area of France that's almost too brill!

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the word falls short by its last letter

blocks.note: too and also are synonyms
brill is British slang for brilliant, as is ace

explanation.surface: A tourist gushes that a French region is just too brilliant.
explanation.walkthrough: Brill is British informal for 'brilliant', though it also looks like the fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Alsace is a region of north-eastern France bordering Germany, known for its wines.

clue.text: Law suit finally disposed of – for a figure

indicators.note: finally points to the very last letter of the word it follows
something disposed of is got rid of, so that letter is removed

blocks.note: a statute is a written law
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A lawsuit has finally been settled over a disputed figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Law suit' reads as one word, lawsuit, but splits into the law and the suit whose last letter goes.
explanation.definitionFit: A statue is a sculpted figure of a person or animal, so figure is a fair synonym.

clue.text: German prince regularly rattled the voters

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every second letter is kept

blocks.note: a prince of the Holy Roman Empire entitled to choose the emperor
the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: A German nobleman shaken up by the voters.
explanation.walkthrough: The Electors were German princes with a vote in choosing the Holy Roman Emperor.
explanation.definitionFit: The electorate is the whole body of people entitled to vote in an election.

clue.text: Stops blowing top and relaxes

indicators.note: blowing its top means losing its head, so the first letter goes in this down clue

blocks.note: ceases means stops

explanation.surface: Someone stops losing their temper and calms down.
explanation.definitionFit: Eases means loosens or lessens tension, so it is a synonym for relaxes.

clue.text: Prison warden blowing his top – nothing new in section of wing

indicators.note: to blow one's top is to lose one's head, so the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: a jailer guards prisoners
zero, shaped like the letter O
standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A furious prison officer loses his temper and is left with nothing new to say.
explanation.definitionFit: An aileron is a hinged flap on the trailing edge of an aircraft wing, controlling roll.

clue.text: Grammatical parity? Yes, of course!

blocks.note: first meaning: the matching of words in number, gender or person
second meaning: an exclamation of assent

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is a stretch, since agreement is a noun and 'Yes, of course!' an expression of it rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar, agreement is the concord of subject and verb; in speech, agreement is consent, as 'Yes, of course' shows.

clue.text: Alternate alternately, before Easter

definitions.note: describes the period rather than naming it

indicators.note: alternately means every other one, so we keep letters in turn and skip the rest

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: A rule to switch back and forth in the run-up to Easter.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated word is self-referential: 'Alternate' is both the source and, via 'alternately', the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Lent is the forty-day Christian season of fasting and penitence that comes just before Easter.

clue.text: Right note, wrong information for physicist

indicators.note: something wrong is not right as it stands, so these letters must be put in another order

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for right
the word rearranged
gen is British slang for information

explanation.surface: A physicist received the right memo but wrong data.
explanation.walkthrough: Wilhelm Roentgen discovered X-rays. 'Wrong information' reads as a phrase, but 'wrong' only works on the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilhelm Roentgen was the German physicist who discovered X-rays and won the first Nobel Prize in Physics.

clue.text: Foremost crossword compiler, almost sweet

indicators.note: almost means falling just short, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: foremost means number one, written No. 1 with the numeral as I
a crossword compiler is called a setter

explanation.surface: The top crossword setter is almost too sweet-natured.
explanation.definitionFit: A noisette is a chocolate sweet flavoured with hazelnuts, from the French for little nut.

clue.text: Husband's trapped in bar, cut off

indicators.note: something trapped inside is held within the surrounding word

blocks.note: bar and save both mean 'except', as in 'all bar one'
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A husband is stuck in a pub and has been cut off by the barman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' is not a pub here but the preposition meaning 'except', the same sense as save.
explanation.definitionFit: To shave is to cut off hair close to the skin, or to trim a thin slice away.

clue.text: Tiger seen wandering – but certainly not here

definitions.note: a cryptic pointer: a place where tigers are not found

indicators.note: letters that wander roam away from their original order

blocks.note: the fodder letters

explanation.surface: Someone reports a tiger spotted roaming loose, but insists it was nowhere near here.
explanation.walkthrough: The Serengeti is an African plain famous for lions and wildebeest; tigers live only in Asia, so a tiger sighting there is impossible.
explanation.definitionFit: The Serengeti is an African savannah, and wild tigers are native only to Asia, so they are never found there.

clue.text: Noble women tot up letters

blocks.note: to tot up is to add up or count
the letter S spelt out, plural

explanation.surface: Aristocratic ladies are adding up their correspondence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letters' looks like correspondence but means the letter S written as a word, several times.
explanation.definitionFit: A countess is a woman holding the rank of earl or count, or an earl's wife, so she is a noblewoman.

clue.text: Infection for the oculist? Yes!

indicators.note: the answer is presented for us inside the following words, sitting across their boundary

blocks.note: runs across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: Asking whether an eye infection is something to take to the eye doctor, and answering yes.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles 'oculist' and 'Yes'; an oculist is fittingly the doctor who treats it.
explanation.definitionFit: A stye is a small bacterial infection of a gland at the edge of an eyelid.

clue.text: T. Greig's men ordered spice

indicators.note: ordered means arranged or sorted, so these letters are put into a new sequence

blocks.note: fodder letters

explanation.surface: Tony Greig, the former England cricket captain, orders his team a spicy meal.
explanation.walkthrough: Tony Greig captained England at cricket in the 1970s; his name is just fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Stem ginger is the young underground stem of the ginger plant, preserved in syrup and used as a spice.

clue.text: Men retire and set out for Roman road

indicators.note: set out in the sense of laid out afresh, so the letters are put into a new pattern

blocks.note: fodder letters
more fodder letters

explanation.surface: Retired men head out for a walk along an old Roman road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And' simply joins the two pieces of fodder. Ermine Street ran from London to Lincoln and York.
explanation.definitionFit: Ermine Street is the name of a major Roman road in Britain linking London to York.

clue.text: Press hack in loco?

blocks.note: to iron is to press clothes
a hack is a riding horse

explanation.surface: A tabloid journalist who seems to have gone crazy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press hack' looks like a journalist and 'loco' like crazy; loco is short for locomotive.
explanation.definitionFit: Iron horse is an old nickname for a steam locomotive, and loco is a short form of locomotive.

clue.text: Pale blue Toyota model scratching parking sign

indicators.note: to scratch something is to strike it out, as a horse is scratched from a race

blocks.note: aqua is a pale greenish blue
the Toyota Prius hybrid car
P is the abbreviation for parking

explanation.surface: A pale blue Toyota scrapes against a parking sign.
explanation.definitionFit: Aquarius, the water carrier, is one of the twelve signs of the zodiac.

clue.text: Adolescent showing support with flipping king's daughter

indicators.note: flipping means turning over, so the words that follow are read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: a tee supports a golf ball
Regan is one of King Lear's daughters

explanation.surface: A sulky adolescent is propped up, with the king's daughter swearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' looks like a mild British oath; the king is Shakespeare's Lear, whose daughters are Goneril, Regan and Cordelia.
explanation.definitionFit: A teenager is someone aged thirteen to nineteen, which is the stage of life called adolescence.

clue.text: Mission one: punctual BBC debate

blocks.note: a quest is a mission
Roman numeral one
on time means punctual

explanation.surface: A target for a TV debate show: get started punctually.
explanation.walkthrough: Question Time is a long-running BBC panel show where politicians face audience questions.
explanation.definitionFit: Question Time is the BBC's flagship topical political discussion programme, a televised debate.

clue.text: A small-holder in the fruit trade

definitions.text: A small-holder in the fruit trade

blocks.clueFragment: A small-holder in the fruit trade
blocks.note: surface reading: a smallholder, someone farming a few acres, who grows fruit for market
setter's reading: a small container that holds soft fruit for sale

explanation.walkthrough: A smallholder is a farmer with a small plot; split as 'small holder' it becomes a little container.
explanation.definitionFit: A punnet is a small square basket or box in which strawberries and other soft fruit are sold.

clue.text: Sign, for example, mounted on car

indicators.note: mounted means raised up, and in a down clue going up means reading the letters bottom to top

blocks.note: e.g. is short for 'for example'
the Mini is a small British car

explanation.surface: A sign, like a badge, fixed onto a car.
explanation.definitionFit: Gemini, the twins, is one of the twelve signs of the zodiac.

clue.text: A river? Certainly not! But it is!

definitions.text: A river? Certainly not! But it is!

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for river
an emphatic refusal

explanation.surface: Someone denies a thing is a river, then admits it is one after all.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay seems to deny it is a river, yet the whole clue then insists it is one: the Arno flows through Florence and Pisa.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arno is a river in Tuscany, Italy, flowing through Florence and Pisa to the sea.

clue.text: Not that tiny now

blocks.note: this is the opposite of that
minute (my-NEWT) means tiny

explanation.surface: Choosing between objects: not that one, the tiny one, right now.
explanation.walkthrough: MINUTE is the adjective meaning tiny, but in the answer it becomes the unit of time.
explanation.definitionFit: This minute is an idiom for immediately, at the present moment, exactly as 'now' says.

clue.text: Fish shoulders, oddly!

indicators.note: oddly means in the odd-numbered positions, so the first, third, fifth letters and so on are kept

blocks.note: letters one, three, five, seven and nine

explanation.surface: An exclamation at a fish that strangely seems to have shoulders.
explanation.definitionFit: Soles are flatfish, a familiar plural for the fish of that name.

clue.text: Cut up skittles

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from bottom to top

blocks.note: skittles are the pins knocked down in bowling

explanation.surface: Chopping up a set of skittles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut up' looks like one phrasal verb, but 'Cut' is the definition and 'up' the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To snip is to cut with small quick strokes of scissors.

clue.text: Popular officer, mainly

blocks.note: in fashion means popular
a high-ranking army officer

explanation.surface: An officer who is, for the most part, well liked by the troops.
explanation.definitionFit: In general is an idiom meaning usually, for the most part, which is what mainly says.

clue.text: Lowdown on the team's spirits

blocks.note: gen is British slang for information, the lowdown
a team of eleven, as in cricket or football, written in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Getting the inside story on how the team's morale is holding up.
explanation.walkthrough: A side is often called an eleven, hence II. Gen is British informal for information.
explanation.definitionFit: Genii is a plural of genie or genius, meaning supernatural spirits like the jinn of Arabian tales.

clue.text: It affects sheep, as price is variable

indicators.note: something variable can change, so these letters take another order

blocks.note: fodder letters

explanation.surface: A farmer notes that fluctuating market prices hit sheep farming hard.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrapie is a fatal brain disease of sheep and goats, making them scrape against posts.

clue.text: Parts of a fugue – one finally started by Stravinsky and completed by Tippett

indicators.note: what something is started by comes at its beginning, so the opening letters are taken
what completes a thing comes at its end, so the closing letters are taken

blocks.note: the first three letters of the composer's name
the last three letters of the composer's name
Roman numeral one, placed at the end

explanation.surface: A fugue begun by Stravinsky and finished off by Tippett, two twentieth-century composers.
explanation.walkthrough: The composer names suit the musical surface, but only their first and last three letters are used.
explanation.definitionFit: Stretti is the plural of stretto, the overlapping of subject entries near the end of a fugue.
